before-money.question: You offer apples for bread, but the baker does not want apples. What could help?
answers: Find another exchange both people agree to
before-money.explanation: A swap needs agreement. You may need a different partner or offer.

before-money.question: A town uses money, swaps and credit. Which conclusion fits?
answers: Every town must abandon barter before using money
Credit means nobody needs to repay
before-money.explanation: Exchange methods can exist together. Credit creates an obligation under agreed terms.

first-coins.question: A trader sees a familiar stamp on an old coin. What does it help them identify?
first-coins.explanation: A stamp identifies an issuer. It does not set all prices or record every owner.

first-coins.question: Why might a stamp alone be insufficient to assess an ancient coin?
answers: All stamped objects have equal value
Weight, metal and trust also matter
A stamp guarantees the price of goods
first-coins.explanation: A stamp supplies one clue. Weight, metal and trust in the issuer also affected acceptance.

strange-money.question: Your pretend town chooses leaves as money. What problem should you consider?
strange-money.explanation: Money that tears or decays is difficult to store and reuse.

strange-money.question: Two objects are accepted as payment. What else helps compare their usefulness as money?
answers: Durability, portability and ease of dividing value
strange-money.explanation: Acceptance matters, but storing, carrying and dividing value also affect everyday use.

money-through-time.question: Which order runs from older to newer payment methods?
money-through-time.explanation: Coins existed before banknotes. Phone payments are much more recent.

money-through-time.question: A shop introduces phone payments and still takes cash. What does this show?
answers: New and older methods can coexist
A phone payment creates extra money
money-through-time.explanation: New technology does not automatically replace every older method. Access and preferences differ.

banknote-lab.question: A pretend banknote has a clear window. Why might a real note use such a feature?
answers: To set the price of toys
To make the note worth more each day
To help people check it and make copying harder
banknote-lab.explanation: Security features support checks. A feature does not determine shop prices or increase the face value.

banknote-lab.question: Two notes have a similar colour. How should you assess whether one is genuine?
answers: Use colour as the only test
Check relevant features using the issuing bank’s official guidance
Assume both are genuine because they look alike
banknote-lab.explanation: Colour alone is insufficient. Different currencies use different features; follow the relevant issuer’s guidance.

gold-vault.question: A coin looks gold-coloured. What can you conclude from the colour alone?
gold-vault.explanation: A gold colour does not prove that an object is made of gold.

gold-vault.question: A coin’s face value exceeds the value of its metal. Which statement fits?
answers: Payment value can differ from material value
The coin cannot function as money
Every coin must be redeemable for gold
gold-vault.explanation: The stated payment value and metal value are different. Modern UK pounds are not redeemable for a fixed quantity of gold.

around-the-world.question: Which country and currency match is correct?
around-the-world.explanation: Japan uses yen. The UK uses pounds sterling.

around-the-world.question: At made-up rates of £1 = 150 yen and later £1 = 160 yen, what does £5 buy, ignoring fees?
around-the-world.explanation: Multiply each rate by 5: 750 and 800 yen. Real exchanges may also have fees.

business-invention.question: You make one bookmark sample. What feedback is most useful next?
answers: Whether a reader finds it easy to use
Whether you can ignore material costs
business-invention.explanation: Ask a relevant user about the sample before spending more. Interest does not guarantee sales.

business-invention.question: A supervised trial sells 8 bookmarks for £2 each. Total costs are £10. What is the profit?

museum-of-mistakes.question: Two customers suggest different changes. What should you do?
answers: Compare their reasons and test a small change
museum-of-mistakes.explanation: Different feedback can reveal different needs. A small test helps you learn before a larger change.

museum-of-mistakes.question: One complaint asks for a costly redesign. What evidence helps you decide?
answers: The complaint alone proves every customer wants it
The cost can be ignored if someone asks
Compare feedback patterns, trial results and costs
museum-of-mistakes.explanation: A complaint is useful evidence, but it does not represent every customer. Check likely benefits and costs.

future-money.question: A pretend account has £5. A £2 debit-card payment is made, with no other transactions. What remains?
Which statement correctly compares debit and credit payments?
answers: Both create money that never needs paying back
Debit uses account funds; credit is borrowing to repay
A phone wallet always means free money
future-money.explanation: Debit uses available account funds in this example. Credit involves borrowing; interest or fees may apply. A wallet is a payment tool.
